title: The Letter With No Return Address

post.author: u/ashgrove_mailroom
post.title: I sort the mail at a hotel overnight. Since Monday, at three in the morning, the hotel forgets every guest it has.

blocks.text: I work the mailroom at the Hotel Ashgrove, eleven to seven. Letters, parcels, and since last year the request slips. Every room has a tablet now. A guest taps *extra blanket*, and the tablet sends a request to the hotel's website. The website is a server: a program on the hotel's computer that waits for requests and answers them. Then a slip prints on my printer with the room number on top. I carry the blanket up.

Bram, our IT man, who looks after the hotel's computers, explained it to me as mail, which I appreciated. Each request is a letter, written in a shared language called HTTP, short for Hypertext Transfer Protocol. It starts with a method, a word saying what you want: GET means *send me something*, POST means *here is something for you*.
Then comes a path saying which page it's about, like /requests. Then headers: extra lines on the envelope, each a name and a value.

The website writes back a letter called a response. On top is a status code, a number saying how it went: 200 means fine, 404 means *no such page*, 503 means *not now, try later*. Under it is the body, the letter itself.

"The website remembers nothing between letters," Bram said. "Every one arrives as if from a stranger." All it sees is the IP address the letter came from, the sender's number on the internet. So when a guest signs in, proving once who they are, the website gives the tablet a cookie: a claim ticket with a number on it, like sid=7f3a.

The website keeps the matching note: *7f3a is room 412*. That note is called a session. It lives in the website's memory, the working space a running program keeps its notes in. The tablet shows its ticket on every letter after that. Each time, the website reads the number, finds the matching note, and knows the room.

Since Monday, this is my printer around three in the morning. Each line shows the time, the method and path, the status code, then what the slip said. A restart means the website is switched off and on again: it stops, stays off for a moment, then starts fresh. Retry-After: 30 is a header meaning *try again in 30 seconds*, so the tablet waits, then sends the letter again:

02:59:41  POST /requests  200  ROOM 412  extra blanket
03:00:00  website restarts (every night)
03:00:12  POST /requests  503  Retry-After: 30
03:00:44  POST /requests  200  ROOM ???  extra blanket
03:00:51  POST /requests  200  ROOM ???  extra blanket
03:00:58  POST /requests  200  ROOM ???  is anyone there

Bram checked the website's log, the diary it writes of every letter. Same tablet. Same ticket, sid=7f3a, on every one of those letters. Room 412 is Mr. Okafor, who has stayed with us for nine years and has never once been called ???. After three, the website looks at his ticket as if it has never seen it before.
A letter with no return address, from a man I can see on the guest list.
Bram says the website restarts at 3:00 every night to stay healthy, and it never mattered until we added the sign-in. What should he change before tonight?

blocks.label: printer_0300.png

diagram.aria: Two minutes around the 3:00 AM restart. The website runs until 03:00:00, restarts for 30 seconds, and runs again from 03:00:30. Room 412's slips say ROOM 412 at 02:59:41. During the restart nothing prints, and a request at 03:00:12 gets 503 with Retry-After: 30. From 03:00:44 the same tablet's slips say ROOM ???.

blocks.caption: Bram's drawing of three o'clock. Before the restart, slips say ROOM 412. During it, the website answers 503 for 30 seconds. After it, the same tablet's slips say ROOM ???.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Look at the 03:00:12 line before the ??? ones. The website told the tablet exactly what was going on and when to come back, and the tablet listened. Then ask Bram where those sessions live, and what happens to anything kept there at 3:00.

replies.author: u/ashgrove_mailroom
replies.text: Bram says the sessions live in the website's memory. Not in the guest database, the program that stores the hotel's records and keeps them through a restart. He went very quiet after he said it.

comments.author: u/front_desk_fiona
comments.text: My last hotel had this, except ours forgot guests at random all day. Turned out there were two copies of the website, and each one only remembered the guests who had signed in on it. A guest signed in on one copy and got a ticket. Their next letter might go to the other copy, which had no note for that ticket, so they were a stranger there.

comments.author: u/packet_ghost
comments.text: The tablet kept its half of the ticket. The website lost its half.

reply.prompt: Bram asks what he should change before tonight's 3:00 restart. Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Add a room number box to the tablet's request form, so every request says which room it's from.
options.part2: Bram added the box. By morning, room 309 had sent two bottles of champagne to room 412's bill. Anyone can write any room number on a letter, and the website believed every one of them. The slips stopped saying ???. They started lying instead.
options.senior: Never let a request simply claim who it's from. A cookie works because it's a random ticket that only the real guest's tablet holds, checked against the hotel's own records.

options.text: Keep the sessions in the hotel's database, which survives a restart, and end each at checkout.
options.part2: Bram moved the sessions into the guest database, which already survives every restart. At 3:00 the website restarted, answered 503 for half a minute, and came back. At 3:01 room 412 asked for a toothbrush, and the slip said ROOM 412. Every tablet's ticket still matched. Sessions now end at checkout. Last night at 3:14 a letter arrived carrying a ticket that ended in March, and the website turned it away, as it should. Bram says the tablet in that room has been unplugged since spring.
options.senior: HTTP forgets you between requests by design. Remembering is your job, and the memory has to live somewhere that outlasts a restart, because restarts, updates and crashes will happen.

options.text: Stop the nightly restart. If the website never restarts, it never forgets who has signed in.
options.part2: No restart on Monday, and no ??? slips. On Wednesday the website crawled from 2 AM. The nightly restart had been hiding a slow leak: the website was using a little more memory every hour. At 4:12 it crashed on its own, every guest was forgotten anyway, and the tablets got 503s for eleven minutes.
options.senior: Removing the restart removes the sign of the problem, not its cause. Websites restart for updates, crashes and moves. Anything kept only in memory will be lost the next time.

options.text: Remember guests by their IP address instead of a cookie, since it comes with every request.
options.part2: Bram tried it on the third floor. Every tablet in the hotel reaches the website through the hotel's one internet connection, so they all arrived with the same address. Room 301 opened its tablet and saw room 412's requests. Bram switched it off at 3:40 AM.
options.senior: An IP address says which network a request came through, not who sent it. Whole hotels, offices and phone networks share one.

sim.title: Write a letter to the hotel's website
sim.lede: You're the tablet in room 412. Build a request: pick a method and a path, choose whether to send your cookie, and send it to the Hotel Ashgrove's website. The response shows its status code, headers and body. The clock runs 3 times faster than real life. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: POST to /login, then GET /requests. Turn the cookie off and ask again: the website has never heard of you. Try /spa and /minibar. Send six requests in a row, quickly. Then restart the website, wait for the 503s to end, and ask again with the cookie on. Last, switch on the database, sign in again, then restart and ask once more.

explain.oneLine: Nothing was wrong with Mr. Okafor's tablet. Its cookie still said 7f3a, but the website kept the matching session in its memory, and the 3:00 AM restart wiped it.

steps.title: HTTP is letters, not a phone call.
steps.text: HTTP is the language web browsers, apps and websites use. A client, the program that asks, sends a request: a method, a path, headers, and sometimes a body. The server reads it, does the work, and sends back a response: a status code, headers and a body. The client reads the status code first to see how it went. Then it's over. If no response comes, the client usually waits a while, then gives up or sends the letter again. The letters usually travel over a TCP connection like the ones in case 3: an open line, set up with a three-call handshake. The tablet can keep that line open and send letter after letter over it, so it doesn't pay for a new handshake every time. HTTP is still stateless, meaning it remembers nothing. Each request has to make sense on its own. The server remembers nothing about the last one unless someone builds that memory on top.

steps.title: Methods say what you want.
steps.text: GET asks for something and changes nothing. POST hands something over, like a new request for a blanket. PUT replaces something with the version you send, and DELETE removes it. Sending the same GET, PUT or DELETE twice leaves things just as sending it once would, like pressing a lift button twice. That is called idempotent. POST isn't, which is why sending a POST twice can print two slips.

steps.title: Status codes say what happened, by family.
steps.text: The first digit is the family, and xx stands for any two digits. 2xx: it worked (200 OK). 3xx: look elsewhere (301 Moved Permanently, with a Location header saying where). 4xx: a problem with your request (404 Not Found, or 429 Too Many Requests when you send too fast). Two 4xx codes are about who you are. 401 Unauthorized means you haven't proved it: no session, or one the server doesn't recognise, so sign in again. 403 Forbidden means the server knows who you are, or doesn't need to, and still won't do it. Room 309 trying to cancel room 412's requests would get one. 5xx: a problem on the server's side (500 Internal Server Error when something broke, 503 Service Unavailable for not now). A 429 or a 503 can carry a Retry-After header saying when to try again, exactly as the website did at 03:00:12.

steps.title: A cookie is a claim ticket. A session is the coat.
steps.text: To remember a guest, the website sends a Set-Cookie header (sid=7f3a) after sign-in. The tablet keeps it and sends it back in a Cookie header on every later request to that site. The cookie is just a ticket number, called the session ID. What the ticket means, *7f3a is room 412*, lives on the server side in a session. On each request, the website reads the ticket number from the Cookie header and looks it up among its sessions. If it finds a match, it knows the guest. If not, the request is treated as a stranger's. Both halves are needed. Without the cookie, the website can't tell who you are, and a cookie with no matching session is no better. And 7f3a is far too easy to guess: four characters like that allow only 65,536 tickets. Real session IDs are long random strings of letters and numbers. OWASP, a web security project, says they need at least 64 bits of randomness. A bit is the smallest piece of computer data, a 0 or a 1. That much randomness means nobody can guess another guest's ticket.

steps.title: The website kept its sessions in memory.
steps.text: The Ashgrove's website stored sessions in its own memory: the fastest place, and the one that empties when the program stops. At 3:00 the nightly restart wiped every session. For 30 seconds the website wasn't running. A small program in front of it, which passes letters through, answered every letter with 503 and Retry-After: 30. A program like that is called a proxy. Then the website came back with an empty memory. Mr. Okafor's tablet still sent 7f3a, which now matched nothing, so his letters were treated as a stranger's and printed ROOM ???.

diagram.aria: The tablet signs in with POST /login. The website saves 7f3a is room 412 in its session memory and answers 200 OK with Set-Cookie: sid=7f3a. Before 3:00, a POST /requests with Cookie: sid=7f3a is looked up, matched to room 412, and the slip says ROOM 412. At 3:00 the restart wipes the memory. After it, the same request with the same cookie finds no session, and the slip says ROOM ???.

steps.text: Same ticket, no session: a stranger

explain.caption: Read top to bottom. The cookie is the tablet's half of the ticket, and the session is the website's half. At 3:00 the website's half vanished. The tablet kept sending 7f3a, and the website had nothing to match it with.

fix.title: The fix: keep sessions where a restart can't reach them
fix.text: Store sessions somewhere that outlives the website program, such as the hotel's database or a store built for sessions. A restart then costs 30 seconds of 503s, not every guest's sign-in. Give every session an end, such as checkout day. Mark the cookie HttpOnly, a setting that stops scripts, small programs running inside the page, from reading it. Treat a request with no valid session as a stranger on purpose. Answer 401 Unauthorized, which tells the tablet to sign in again, instead of printing ROOM ???. Make session IDs long and random, not short like 7f3a. And have clients handle 503 and 429 politely: wait as long as Retry-After says, then try again, instead of hammering the door.

limits: A database for sessions is one more thing that can be slow or down. And every request now waits while the website looks the session up. Teams keep that lookup fast and plan for what happens when the store is unavailable.

The cookie is the whole key. Anyone who copies it can act as that guest until the session ends. That's why sessions should expire, and cookies should travel only over encrypted connections, scrambled so only the two ends can read them. The next case covers those.

Retrying, sending a failed request again, can make things worse. If every client retries the instant it sees a 5xx, a struggling server gets hit harder. Clients should wait longer after each failure, add a little randomness, and give up after a few tries.

head: Where sessions live
Good
Bad
rows: Lost on every restart or crash. Only that one copy of the website knows them.
In a database or session store
Survives restarts. Every copy of the website can read it.
One more system to run, and a lookup on every request.
The cookie carries the session itself, stamped so any change shows. The server stores nothing at all.
Hard to end a session early, and the cookie grows. A later season covers this.

explain.seniorTake: HTTP forgets you between letters on purpose. That's what lets any server answer any request. Memory is something you add, and where you put it decides what a restart costs. Read status codes as instructions. 4xx: fix your letter. 5xx: not your fault. 429 and 503: wait and come back.

realWorld.title: RFC 9110: the rules of the letter
realWorld.text: Internet rules are written down in numbered documents called RFCs, short for Request for Comments. HTTP's meaning is set out in RFC 9110, published in June 2022. It defines HTTP as a stateless protocol, a set of rules where each request can be understood on its own. It defines the methods GET, POST, PUT and DELETE. It marks GET as safe, meaning it changes nothing, and GET, PUT and DELETE as idempotent. It sets out the five status code families from 1xx to 5xx, including 301, 401, 403, 404, 500 and 503. It defines 401 as a request that lacks valid proof of who is asking, and 403 as one the server understood but refuses to carry out. MDN, Mozilla's free guide to the web, lists the same codes in plain words.

realWorld.title: 429 and Retry-After
realWorld.text: 429 Too Many Requests comes from RFC 6585, published in April 2012. It means the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time. Capping requests like that is called rate limiting. The response may include a Retry-After header saying how long to wait before asking again.

realWorld.title: Cloudflare, November 18, 2025
realWorld.text: At 11:20 UTC (the world clock engineers share), Cloudflare's network, which sits in front of many websites, began failing to deliver traffic. Visitors saw an error page pointing to a failure inside Cloudflare's network. A change to who could see what in a database had made a configuration file, a file of settings, double in size. The file belonged to Bot Management, Cloudflare's system for telling automated traffic from people. It grew past a limit in the software that reads it. The file was rebuilt every five minutes, sometimes good and sometimes bad. So Cloudflare's graph of 5xx errors spiked, recovered and spiked again, and at first the team suspected an attack. Core traffic was largely flowing again by 14:30 UTC, and everything was normal by 17:06 UTC. Every one of those 5xx answers told visitors the truth: the problem was on the server side, not in their requests.

realWorld.title: How AWS's own SDKs handle 5xx and throttling
realWorld.text: AWS is Amazon Web Services, Amazon's rented computers and services. Its SDKs, short for software development kits, are ready-made code that programs use to call AWS. AWS's guide to them describes how they react to these codes. Some errors are passing ones, including any HTTP 500, 502, 503 or 504. Others are throttling errors, AWS's name for too many requests. Both are retried automatically, with 3 attempts in all by default. Each wait is longer than the last, called exponential backoff, plus a little randomness, called jitter. Errors a retry can't fix, such as a request with bad details in it, come back at once. A retry quota, a budget of retries, makes a client stop retrying when failures are widespread. It fails fast instead of piling onto a struggling service. The guide notes that some details are changing with updated retry behavior in 2026.

asked: What's the difference between a 4xx and a 5xx error, and what should a client do with each?
HTTP is stateless. So how does a website keep you logged in?
interview.answer: 4xx means the request was the problem: a wrong path (404), no valid sign-in (401), not allowed (403), or too many requests (429). Fix the request rather than retrying. For 401, sign in again. For 403, signing in again won't help. The exception is 429, which says wait and try again, often with Retry-After. 5xx means the server failed. Retrying can help for 502, 503 and 504. But wait longer each time (exponential backoff), add a little randomness (jitter), set a limit, and only repeat requests that are safe to repeat. HTTP keeps no memory between requests. So after sign-in, the server uses Set-Cookie to send a cookie holding a long random session ID. The browser sends it back in the Cookie header, and the server looks the session up. Then say where the session lives. Kept in one server's memory, it dies with a restart and other servers can't see it. So real systems serving real users use a shared store, or a signed token: a ticket that carries the session itself, stamped so any change shows.

terms.def: Hypertext Transfer Protocol: the language of the web. A client sends a request, a server sends back a response, and that's the whole conversation.
A server program that answers HTTP requests with pages and data, like the hotel's guest site.
The letter a client sends: a method, a path, headers, and sometimes a body.
The letter the server sends back: a status code, headers and a body.
The first word of a request, saying what you want done: GET, POST, PUT or DELETE are the common ones.
The method for asking for something without changing anything, like opening a page.
The method for handing something over to be processed, like a new blanket request or a sign-in. Sending it twice can do the thing twice.
The method for replacing something with the version you send. Sending the same PUT twice ends the same as sending it once.
The method for removing something.
The part of the address after the site name that says which page or thing you mean, like /requests or /login.
An extra line on a request or response, written as name: value, like Retry-After: 30. The writing on the envelope.
The content of a request or response: the page, the data, or the message itself.
A three-digit number at the top of every response saying how the request went, like 200, 404 or 503.
The first digit of a status code: 1xx information, 2xx success, 3xx look elsewhere, 4xx a problem with the request, 5xx a problem on the server's side.
The request worked.
The page has a new address for good. The Location header gives the new one.
You haven't proved who you are: no session, or one the server doesn't recognise. Sign in and try again. Despite its name, it's about who you are, not what you may do.
The server knows who you are, or doesn't need to, and still refuses, like room 309 asking to cancel room 412's requests. Signing in again won't help.
The server has nothing at that path.
The path exists, but not for that method, like sending DELETE to a page that only allows GET. The Allow header lists the methods that work.
You sent too many requests in a short time, and the server is limiting you. It may say when to try again with Retry-After.
Something broke inside the server while it was answering. Not the client's fault.
The server can't handle requests right now, because it's restarting, under maintenance or overloaded. Often comes with Retry-After.
Any status code from 500 to 599: the server side failed, not the request.
The header on a 3xx response that gives the address to go to instead.
A header on a 429 or 503 saying how many seconds to wait before trying again.
A header saying what kind of body this is, like text/plain for plain text or text/html for a web page.
The header on a 405 response listing the methods that path accepts.
Remembering nothing between requests. Each HTTP request must carry everything the server needs to understand it.
A small named value a website asks the browser to keep and send back on every later request to that site, like a claim ticket: sid=7f3a.
The response header a server uses to hand the browser a cookie.
The request header the browser uses to send its cookies back to the site.
The server's record of who a cookie belongs to, like 7f3a is room 412. The cookie is the ticket, the session is the coat it claims.
The random ticket number inside the cookie that points to one session. Real ones are long, with at least 64 bits of randomness, so nobody can guess them. 7f3a is a short stand-in.
A non-profit web security project whose free guides, such as its Session Management Cheat Sheet, are a standard reference for building safe websites.
The smallest piece of computer data: a 0 or a 1. Each extra random bit doubles the guesses needed, so 64 random bits allow about 18 billion billion values.
Proving who you are once, after which the website gives you a session cookie so you don't have to prove it again on every request.
A cookie setting that keeps scripts on the web page from reading the cookie. Only HTTP requests carry it.
A cookie that carries the session data itself, stamped so the server can tell if anyone changed it. The server then stores nothing.
Doing it twice ends the same as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are meant to be idempotent. POST isn't.
A method that only reads and changes nothing on the server, like GET.
Where a running program keeps its working data. Fast, but emptied when the program stops or restarts.
A program that sits in front of another and passes requests through. When the program behind it is down, it can answer for it, for example with 503.
Capping how many requests one client may send in a period of time. Requests over the cap get 429.
AWS's word for rate limiting: slowing or refusing a client that sends too much.
Sending a failed request again. Safe for idempotent requests. Risky for POST, which may run twice.
Waiting longer after each failed try, for example 1, 2, then 4 seconds, so a struggling server gets room to recover.
A little randomness added to retry waits, so thousands of clients don't all retry at the same instant.
A budget of retries in an AWS SDK. When failures are widespread it runs out, and the client stops retrying and fails fast.
Software development kit: a library programmers use to call a service, like AWS's SDKs for Python or Java.
Putting a new version of a program live, which usually restarts it.
A file of settings a program reads to decide how to behave.
Cloudflare's feature for telling automated traffic from people.
An AWS service that receives HTTP requests and spreads them across several servers, called targets. It reports how many 4xx and 5xx responses it and its targets sent.

atWork: Your team may run a web service on AWS, Amazon's rented computers, behind an Application Load Balancer: an AWS service that takes incoming requests and shares them out across several servers. If so, open the load balancer's Monitoring tab in the EC2 console, the web page where AWS lists your rented servers. Read-only access is enough. Over the last day, compare the 5xx count sent by the load balancer itself with the 4xx and 5xx counts sent by your targets, the servers behind it. Find the biggest spike and ask whose problem it was: the clients' or yours? Then find out where your service keeps sessions. It could be one server's memory, a database, a cache (a store of saved copies), or a signed cookie. Work out what a restart would do to everyone signed in.

recall.prompt: Your team's website logs everyone out every time it's deployed, meaning every time a new version is put live. People sign back in and everything works until the next deploy. What's probably happening, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Sessions are kept in the server's memory and wiped when it restarts
The browser's cookie still arrives but matches no session
Store sessions somewhere that survives restarts

recall.model: The sessions almost certainly live in the website's memory. A deploy restarts the program, the memory is wiped, and every browser's cookie now points to a session that no longer exists, so everyone looks like a stranger. Move sessions to a store that survives restarts, such as a database or a session store, or use signed cookies, so a deploy costs a short pause instead of everyone's sign-in.

recall.prompt: Which status code family means the problem is on the server's side?
recall.why: 5xx codes, like 500 and 503, say the server failed. 4xx codes say the request itself was the problem.

recall.prompt: A client gets 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After: 30. What should it do?
options: Retry at once, in a loop, until it works
Give up for good: the page is gone
recall.why: 429 means you're sending too fast. Retry-After says how long to wait. Retrying at once only adds to the pile and keeps you limited.

recall.prompt: A coworker says: HTTP is stateless, so our site can't know who's logged in unless users type their password on every page. What's the missing piece?

keyIdeas.idea: After sign-in the server sets a cookie, which the browser sends back on every request
The server keeps a session that the cookie points to
Stateless means each request carries what's needed, not that nothing can be remembered

recall.model: Stateless means each request must carry everything the server needs. It doesn't mean nothing can be remembered. After sign-in, the server sends a cookie holding a random session ID with Set-Cookie. The browser sends it back in the Cookie header on every request, and the server looks up the session to see who it is. The password is typed once.

recall.prompt: The tablet asks for /spa and gets 301 Moved Permanently with Location: /wellness. What does that mean?
options: The spa is closed for good
The server broke while looking for the spa
The page has moved for good: ask for /wellness instead
The tablet has to sign in first
recall.why: 3xx means look elsewhere. 301 says the move is permanent, and the Location header gives the new path.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Bram moved the sessions into the database, and the hotel stopped forgetting guests at 3 AM. Now there's a new booking app. When a booking gets a 503, or no answer within one second, the app sends the same POST /bookings again every 100 milliseconds, ten times a second, until something comes back. Friday was a slow night for the website, and three guests were booked twice. Bram's plan: make the website faster.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to the person who wrote the post. What's really going wrong, and what should the app do instead?

keyIdeas.idea: Slow isn't failed: the first POST often worked, and POST isn't idempotent, so the retry booked twice
Respect Retry-After and back off with a little randomness instead of retrying every 100 ms
Make the retry safe: a unique booking ID the server checks, so a repeat is recognized

coldCase.model: A slow answer isn't a failed one. The first POST /bookings often went through, and because POST isn't idempotent, sending it again made a second booking. Retrying every 100 milliseconds also piles more load onto a website that is already struggling, which makes it slower still. The app should wait as long as a 503's Retry-After says, and otherwise wait longer after each try with a little randomness, giving up after a few attempts. And make the retry safe: give each booking a unique ID from the app and have the server refuse a second booking with the same ID. A faster website helps, but it fixes neither problem.
